chapter: Raymond Scott, Kirby and postwar bands
title: A 1944 Hollywood film and roommate Ernie Caceres
summary: Leeman recalls a small part in a film with Charlie Barnet and sharing a room with Ernie Caceres, an underrated clarinetist and baritonist he recommended to Woody Herman.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: You mentioned a couple of films -- we mentioned one film, was there anything you wanted to mention about the era, I want you to talk about your eras.

I did a little picture with Charlie Barnet once where they gave me a little acting part, which was nothing. I think they wiped that off the face of the earth, they don't play it -- it was called "Juke Box Jennie". I had about three or four minutes in that one.
That was 1945.
Yeah, the Sensations of '45, but we made it in '44.
Yes, we did.
And that's where I was taken, and the draft was on in Hollywood -- Ernie Caceres, he and I went together, we were roommates.
Ernie Caceres was what kind of player?
He was a saxophone player.
Thank you.

And never did get any recognition for being the great clarinetist that he was. He was mostly known for his baritone playing, all the records he made with Bobby Hackett and in that era. I got him -- what we needed, we lost the first saxophone player, and I mentioned him to Woody, and he hired him. He was never so happy in his life; nobody had any idea that he could play lead. Now he had been in the
Glenn Miller band.
He was of Mexican-American descent, wasn't he?
Yes.
I think we should mention that.

Yes, and he had a brother, he had two brothers -- Emilio, who was a great jazz violinist, but he never got out of that Texas era. He got back to New York years before I had met Ernie, but the whole family were artistes, and they used to have a little Mexican band within the family, and they used to go around ...
He decided to call it the Mexican-American Wetbacks at that time.
Well, that word came later on to me. I never associated it with that -- and they still call them that.
Right.
They still do that in Texas; they say the wetbacks are coming, and you know, there's that little bristle that goes up and down my spine. Just another part of the racial thing.
So what was that era now?
What year?
Yeah.
It was in '44. And he went into the draft, he went to Fort Dix, and I was deferred. He was just
before me.
When did you go into Eddie Condon's?
Did you want to go into that era, or do you want to talk about something else?
